Forest (coefficient) plot

Source: R/coefficient_plot.R
coefficient_plot.Rd

Draws a horizontal point-and-interval ("forest") plot of model estimates. The input can be a fitted model (anything tidy_estimates() understands) or a data frame of pre-computed estimates.

Usage

coefficient_plot(
  x,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  intercept = FALSE,
  order = c("none", "ascending", "descending"),
  labels = NULL,
  interaction = c("times", "asterisk", "colon", "space"),
  point_colour = depictr_brand(),
  reference_colour = depictr_reference(),
  reference_line = if (exponentiate) 1 else 0,
  point_size = 2.2,
  line_size = 0.7,
  facet = FALSE,
  scales = c("fixed", "free"),
  standardise = FALSE,
  sd_multiple = 1,
  exponentiate = FALSE,
  title = NULL,
  subtitle = NULL,
  x_lab = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A fitted model or a tidy data frame of estimates.

conf_level

Confidence/credible level, passed to tidy_estimates() when x is a model: a single number strictly between 0 and 1.

intercept

Whether to keep the intercept term. Defaults to FALSE, since the intercept is seldom of interest on a forest plot and its scale often overwhelms the other terms.

order

Order of the terms. "ascending" puts the smallest estimate at the bottom and the largest at the top, so estimates increase up the axis. "descending" does the reverse, and "none" keeps model order from top to bottom. The faceted layout (facet = TRUE) stacks its panels the other way up.

labels

Optional display labels for the terms. An unnamed vector gives one label per term in model order (the order tidy_estimates() returns, after the intercept is dropped unless intercept = TRUE), whatever order is. A named vector mapping raw term names to labels, such as c(soil_ph = "Soil pH"), is safer. If NULL, the coefficient of a factor level is labelled with its variable and level, inside interaction terms too, so the contrast of enhanced with the reference level reads treatment: enhanced. Other names are tidied with format_terms().

interaction

Passed to format_terms() to control how interaction terms are rendered (ignored when labels is supplied).

point_colour, reference_colour

Colours for the estimates and the reference line.

reference_line

Position of a vertical reference line. Defaults to 0, or to 1 when exponentiate = TRUE, where a ratio of 1 means no effect. Use NA to omit it.

point_size, line_size

Size of the points and interval lines.

facet

Whether to give each term its own panel with a free x-axis, laid out one per row. This removes the squish that occurs when terms live on very different scales (for example a large intercept alongside small slopes). Defaults to FALSE, preserving the shared-axis layout. A convenience alias for scales = "free".

scales

Either "fixed" (the default, a single shared x-axis) or "free" (one free-scaled panel per term). When facet = TRUE this is forced to "free".

standardise

Whether to scale each coefficient by the spread of its inputs, following Gelman (2008). A continuous input (numeric, with more than two distinct values) is scaled by sd_multiple times its standard deviation in the rows the model used, so its slope becomes the change in the outcome per SD. Factor, character, logical and two-valued numeric inputs (0/1, say) are left unscaled, since a contrast already compares two groups and its per-SD value would depend on how balanced the groups happen to be. An interaction is scaled through its inputs: rainfall:treatment by the SD of rainfall, and a product of two continuous inputs by both their SDs. Matrix-valued terms such as poly() and ns() are left unscaled, with a message. An interaction of continuous inputs draws a warning unless they are all centred. Otherwise, each input's main effect is its slope where the others are zero, and Gelman's remedy is to centre the inputs and refit. A continuous slope and a contrast are comparable only roughly, most nearly with sd_multiple = 2. Requires a fitted model (ignored, with a warning, for a tidy data frame). Defaults to FALSE.

sd_multiple

How many standard deviations of a continuous input one unit of the standardised scale spans when standardise = TRUE. Defaults to 1. Use 2 for Gelman's (2008) convention, under which the coefficient of a continuous input is comparable to that of a balanced binary one.

exponentiate

Whether to draw the exponentiated estimates and intervals on a log10 axis, which shows the coefficients of a logistic regression as odds ratios and those of a Poisson or negative binomial model as rate ratios. It applies after standardise, so a standardised slope becomes a ratio per SD of its predictor. A data frame x must hold estimates on the link scale. Defaults to FALSE.

title, subtitle, x_lab

Plot title, subtitle and x-axis label. x_lab defaults to "Estimate", or, when standardise, "Estimate per SD of predictor" ("per 2 SD" with sd_multiple = 2), followed by "(contrasts unscaled)" when a factor or binary term is drawn. The label names the convention on the figure itself, because only the predictors are rescaled here: a fully standardised beta would rescale the outcome too. With exponentiate = TRUE, "Estimate" gives way to the name of the ratio: "Odds ratio" for a logit link, "Rate ratio" for a log link in a Poisson, quasi-Poisson or negative binomial model, "Risk ratio" for a binomial model with a log link and "exp(Estimate)" otherwise. The last covers an lm(log(y) ~ x) slope, whose exponential is a ratio of geometric means.

Value

A ggplot2::ggplot object.

References

Gelman A (2008). “Scaling regression inputs by dividing by two standard deviations.” Statistics in Medicine, 27(15), 2865–2873. doi:10.1002/sim.3107 .

Examples

fit <- lm(yield ~ rainfall + fertiliser + soil_ph + treatment,
          data = crop_yield)
coefficient_plot(fit)


# Order terms and add a title
coefficient_plot(fit, order = "descending", title = "Drivers of crop yield")


# When an intercept or large term squishes the rest, give each term its own
# free-scaled panel:
coefficient_plot(fit, intercept = TRUE, facet = TRUE)


# Or scale the continuous slopes per SD of their predictors, leaving the
# treatment contrast in the outcome's units:
coefficient_plot(fit, standardise = TRUE)


# Odds ratios from a logistic regression, on a log axis with the line at 1:
gfit <- glm(accuracy ~ word_frequency + condition,
            data = lexical_decision, family = binomial)
coefficient_plot(gfit, exponentiate = TRUE)
